answer: The prevalence of gardening-introduced non-native plants is strongly and systematically habitat-dependent, forming a clear gradient across the ten most widespread habitat types of Barcelona province. Occupancy prevalence (proportion of sampled plots containing at least one gardening-introduced non-native species) is highest in anthropogenic and moisture-rich habitats — Wetlands (50% of plots, 95% Wilson CI 35–65%), Urban (48%, 36–60%), Coastal (45%, 28–62%), and Riparian (36%, 25–49%) — intermediate in Croplands (21%, 14–30%), and very low in Meadows (8%), Coniferous forests (6.5%), Broad-leaved forests (4.4%), Scrublands (1.9%), and Rock outcrops (0%). The habitat effect is highly significant overall (chi-square = 139.4, df = 9, p = 1.3e-25, Cramér's V = 0.47; logistic McFadden R² = 0.24) and persists after controlling for elevation, urbanization, historical cropland, road/stream distance, and climate (habitat likelihood-ratio χ² = 58.5, p = 2.7e-9), with the habitat ranking essentially unchanged (Spearman ρ = 0.98 v. unadjusted); lower elevation and higher rainfall additionally raise occurrence, whereas urbanization alone is non-significant once habitat is accounted for. Complementing this, gardening is the dominant modern introduction pathway regionally (75% of 1985–2019 introductions, up from 17% pre-1500) and the most species-rich pathway in the province (42 of 81 species), yet gardening-introduced species are individually less widespread than unintentionally introduced ones — occupying fewer habitat types even after phylogenetic correction (PGLS coefficient = −1.10, t = −2.54, p = 0.013). Overall, gardening-introduced non-native plants are most prevalent in anthropized and moist habitat types (urban, wetland, coastal, riparian) and largely absent from dry, rocky, and forested habitats, and they behave as habitat specialists rather than broad generalists.

payload.workflow: 1) Read invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, habitat-resolved) as primary prevalence dataset; invasion_success_pathways.csv (81 species) for species-level companion; temporal_trends for framing; phylogenetic_tree.txt for PGLS. 2) Primary metric: occupancy prevalence = % plots with n.gard>0 per habitat (Wilson 95% CI); secondary mean n.gard (bootstrap CI) and relative dominance n.gard/n.total. 3) Unadjusted tests: chi-square (chi2=139.4, p=1.3e-25, Cramer V=0.470); logistic presence~habitat (McFadden R2=0.243) with 45 pairwise contrasts BH-adjusted (22 significant); Poisson count LRT (chi2=196.1, overdispersion phi=1.14); NB vs ZINB (ZINB better, llf -333 vs -500). 4) Diagnostics: Moran's I permutation test on residuals (inverse-distance 50km; I~0.01-0.03, p<0.05); VIF among standardized covariates (elevation 12.9, temperature 18.5 collinear). 5) Adjusted logistic model adding elevation, urban/cropland 2009 (1000m), road/stream distance, temperature, rainfall, and 1956-2009 landscape-change proxy; habitat LRT given covariates chi2=58.5 p=2.7e-9; marginal occupancy predicted per habitat; rank stability rho=+0.976; drop-temperature robustness check gives identical conclusions. 6) Species companion: Kruskal-Wallis/Mann-Whitney on invaded plots, 10km AOO, habitat.range, niche breadth, mrt; PGLS (Brownian covariance from Newick) for habitat.range (gardening coef -1.10, p=0.013). 7) Temporal framing: gardening share 17% (pre-1500) -> 75% (1985-2019). All steps executed in analysis.py; outputs in results/.
